Header
Date: 2026-03-28 | Start: 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Kai Nakamura (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Zenith PM), Raj Patel (Zenith Lead ML Eng), Maya Chen (Data Eng), Owen Lee (Security)
Recording id: ff_20260328_zenith_01

Topics auto-detected: benchmarks, golden prompts, hallucination checks, format validation, scoring approach, timeline.

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'll be the AE coordinating the POC and Kai will lead the bench work.
[00:28] Lena: Hi all, lena here, product lead for the recommendation product. We're trying to validate that an LLM can be used for narrative summaries and reranking for our analytics reports, with tight format constraints.
[00:52] Kai: thanks, lena. Real quick — can you confirm the primary success criteria from your side? Is it latency, correctness, hallucination rate, or some combined business metric?
[01:10] Lena: Good question. From a product lens: first, format fidelity — JSON schema must be followed for 95% of cases. Second, hallucinations must be below our tolerance, we roughly estimate tolerable at 1 per 1,000 responses for high-sensitivity reports. Third, p95 latency under 800ms for single-request sync path. Cost is a tie-breaker.
[01:45] Raj: I want to add throughput: during peak we expect bursts to 120 QPS for summary endpoints, average payload ~700 tokens in, ~350 tokens out. Also want determinism on structured fields.
[02:10] Maya: we'll provide sampling of production records but anonymized. think ~500 rows to start.
[02:34] Owen: security question up front — any requirement for customer-managed KMS? We will need to see encryption at rest and in transit, and RBAC in the console.
[02:55] Ava: noted, we'll send SOC2 and KMS integration docs. Kai, can you outline the bench plan?
[03:12] Kai: sure. Proposed seed bench: three model candidates — one open quantized variant, one medium-sized open model, and Redwood-hosted optimized runtime variant. We'll run: latency (p50/p95), throughput various concurrencies, tokens-per-second, and cost estimates normalized per 1k output tokens. We'll also do quality scoring against a golden prompt set — exact-match for structured fields, normalized F1 for name/entity fields, plus a hallucination flag per response.
[03:49] Lena: what's the golden prompt set? who builds it?
[04:05] Kai: typically a collaboration. We'll start with a 1,000-item golden set seeded by Redwood using canonical prompt templates plus some noise to simulate edge cases. You (Zenith) will supply 200 high-priority prompts — those become the 'critical golden prompts' and go into the regression playlist.
[04:34] Raj: does the skew of prompts matter? we have many short ones and a tail of long ones. should we weight them?
[04:48] Kai: yes, we'll stratify: 60% typical, 30% long-form, 10% adversarial or malformed. That will drive the bench to reflect your distribution.
[05:05] Ava: let's define the scoring rubric now — what metrics make a pass / fail?
[05:21] Lena: for product: 95% format conformance, hallucination rate <0.1% on critical set, and a minimum average quality score (we can use a 0-5 scale) of 4.0 on the golden set. Latency targets p95 <800ms on hosted path, less strict for bulk async jobs.
[05:50] Kai: we'll compute a composite score: QualityScore = 0.6 * (normalized golden-set quality) + 0.25 * (format adherence) + 0.15 * (inverse hallucination rate metric). We'll map it to a 0-100 scale and agree a pass threshold, say 75. We'll also report separate slices for business stakeholders.
[06:26] Raj: can we have an automated hallucination detector? manual labeling is expensive.
[06:38] Kai: yes, semi-automated: use heuristics plus an LLM-based verifier that checks factual assertions against the provided context, and then sample for human review on flagged items. For structured fields we can run schema validators and regex checks — those are deterministic.
[06:59] Maya: what about edge-case formatting? sometimes the model returns stray commas, or string instead of list. regex isn't enough.
[07:12] Kai: we'll implement a format-validation pipeline: JSON schema validator + post-parse rules (type coercion, missing keys). Any coercion counts as partial fail in the scoring. We can include unit tests per field.
[07:37] Owen: I heard mention of private deployment in your docs — do we need that for the POC? data residency concerns maybe.
[07:48] Ava: for POC we can run on hosted with VPC peering or Redwood Dedicated if you need isolation. Owen, what's your bar?
[07:58] Owen: ideally customer-managed keys and dedicated nodes for the pilot; if not possible, we need strict audit logs and flow of PII to be blocked. We'll review your SOC2 controls.
[08:16] Kai: operationally, bench harness will mark any record with sensitive PII and we can mask before sending to the model. Also we can run the bench in your VPC if you prefer — that's available but needs extra lead time to provision.
[08:37] Lena: timeline expectation? how long to get results?
[08:44] Ava: propose this timeline — now until 2026-03-31: exchange data and golden prompts; 2026-04-01 to 2026-04-03 seed benchmark run; 2026-04-06 to 2026-04-17 two-week pilot including regression and human spot checks; 2026-04-20: review meeting and decision. Does that fit?
[09:10] Raj: yes that seems reasonable, assuming benchmarking environment mirrors production QPS.
[09:21] Kai: we'll need the concurrency profiles and average tokens/request to emulate production. Raj, you said 700 in / 350 out avg?
[09:31] Raj: correct. Also some long reports up to 2,000 tokens in rare cases. We'll mark those as 'bulk' for async flow.
[09:42] Kai: okay will include bulk test runs with long sequence lengths to test KV cache and memory pressure.
[09:50] Lena: about regression tests — what's the cadence? weekly? after model changes?
[10:00] Kai: for the POC, regression playlist run nightly during the 2-week pilot with daily alerts for regressions on critical prompts. Post-POC we recommend running regression on every model or prompt change.
[10:15] Maya: how do you detect regressions quantitatively?
[10:20] Kai: we set a baseline score per prompt. A regression is triggered if a prompt drops beyond a stat threshold (e.g., >5 point drop in quality score) or if format conformance drops below 95% for critical prompts. We'll surface diffs and sample responses for human review.
[10:41] Owen: audit logs — can you retain per-request traces for how you scored hallucination checks? We need that for compliance.
[10:51] Ava: yes, Redwood Console will keep per-request traces; retention policy can be adjusted as an add-on. We'll pass details to Owen.
[11:02] Lena: tooling — do you have an eval harness we can run, or is it Redwood-run only?
[11:09] Kai: we have a self-hostable eval harness (open source-ish) that runs the bench and regression tests. For the POC we'll run initially on Redwood infra and we can provide the harness to run in your environment later.
[11:28] Lena: good. on scoring metrics — you mentioned exact match for structured fields and normalized F1 for others. Can you clarify normalization?
[11:38] Kai: normalized F1 is token-level F1 with simple normalization rules (lowercase, strip punctuation, canonicalize dates). For structured keys, exact match after normalization. We'll publish the scoring script so it's deterministic.
[11:56] Raj: what about hallucination scoring — is it binary?
[12:02] Kai: binary per assertion for detection, but the final hallucination score is percentage of asserted facts flagged as hallucinated. We'll weight hallucination on critical prompts more heavily in composite score.
[12:18] Lena: folks often see models 'confidently wrong' — do you run calibration checks?
[12:25] Kai: we can check confidence proxies (logits or softmax when available), but for blackbox models we rely on calibration via verifier models and human labels. We'll include a calibration report in the bench.
[12:45] Owen: security follow-up, small item — IP allowlist, SAML/SSO for console access, and KMS key wrap options.
[12:55] Ava: we'll include SAML docs and KMS options in the packet.
[13:04] Lena: OK, about golden prompts — we want to include edge cases we see in production, like corrupted CSV blobs.
[13:15] Kai: absolutely. We'll include adversarial set and malformed inputs as separate slice in the regression playlist and they count heavily for format conformance metric.
[13:33] Maya: can we test temperature and decoding knobs as part of bench? e.g., top_k/top_p and sampling vs deterministic?
[13:44] Kai: yes, we'll sweep decoding parameters to see effect on hallucination/format adherence, and capture tradeoffs in the scorecard. We'll show cost per configuration.
[13:58] Lena: how will the results be presented? one pager? spreadsheet?
[14:04] Kai: we'll deliver a benchmark spreadsheet with per-prompt results, aggregate scorecard, time-series plots of regressions, and a final recommendation: green/orange/red per model. Also a reproducible artifact (bench scripts + seed data).
[14:26] Raj: important: include token-level cost breakdown and estimated monthly cost at our expected QPS.
[14:34] Kai: yes cost modeling included. We'll assume your token mix and project monthly usage at 100% traffic to give an upper bound.
[14:47] Lena: one more product ask: we want to measure 'instruction-following fidelity' — i.e., obeying user provided constraints like "do not hallucinate sources".
[14:58] Kai: we'll include instruction-abidance tests in the golden set, with scoring for explicit instruction violations.
[15:10] Ava: ok lets talk handoffs — after the bench run, we should meet to go over deck and decide whether to expand to dedicated nodes.
[15:17] Lena: yes.
[15:20] Kai: quick note on KV cache — for long form summarization the KV cache hit rate and memory are key. We'll instrument that and report effective tokens/sec when cache warm.
[15:36] Raj: can you simulate warm/cold cache?
[15:39] Kai: yes, bench steps will include cold start and warmed scenarios.
[15:45] Owen: regulatory note — any logs containing PII must be redacted before leaving our network. Is that possible?
[15:53] Kai: yes, we can run redaction rules pre-send or run the bench inside your VPC so logs never leave. We'll coordinate with Maya on masking rules.
[16:05] Maya: we'll provide a redaction spec.
[16:10] Ava: great. any other blockers?
[16:13] Lena: none from product.
[16:15] Raj: need to confirm compute availability windows for the bench — we prefer bench runs outside peak business hours but need realistic concurrency.
[16:25] Kai: understood, we'll schedule runs in your off-peak with a stress test during placeholder peak windows.
[16:36] Ava: ok last section: acceptance criteria and go/no-go decision. How do we reflect business impact?
[16:44] Lena: go if composite score >=75 AND p95 latency <800ms AND format conformance >=95% on critical set. If any of those fail, we consider remediation (quantization change, caching, or model variant) before go.
[17:06] Kai: we'll produce remediation recommendations too — e.g., quantize, change beam/sampling, or move to Dedicated nodes.
[17:18] Owen: and from security if KMS & audit logs meet our bar, we clear that box. Otherwise may need dedicated nodes.
[17:28] Ava: good. I'll capture these next steps and circulate minutes. Anything else?
[17:33] Lena: can you include an example scoring sheet in the packet?
[17:37] Kai: will attach a sample scoring sheet with formulas.
[17:41] Maya: will send sample dataset by 2026-03-31.
[17:46] Raj: will add concurrency profile and extreme-value examples.
[17:51] Owen: will review SOC2 docs and follow up on KMS by 2026-03-31.
[17:58] Ava: ok thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and schedule the bench kickoff.
